title: Stories that answer behavioural questions
objectives: Build six stories in situation, task, action and result form that cover the common behavioural questions.

screens.title: Label the story
screens.prose: Tom was asked "Tell me about a time you failed." Here is his answer, one sentence a row. Label each sentence with the letter of the part it plays.

rows: Task: what was yours to do

screens.question: Type S, T, A or R beside each sentence.

rows: Last year I entered a university trading competition with two friends.
Teams traded a simulated market for three weeks with £100,000 of play money.
My job was to set our risk limits and keep us inside them.
I set the limits on day one, then stopped checking them.
In week two one position reached four times its limit and lost £18,000.
I closed it the next morning and told my teammates what I had missed.
I then wrote a check of every position against its limit, run twice a day.
We finished 9th of 40 teams, and no limit was broken again.

hints.text: S is where and when; T is the job Tom had.
Sentences 4, 6 and 7 start with "I" and a verb.
S, S, T, A, R, A, A, R.

feedback.correct: S, S, T, A, R, A, A, R.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask of each sentence: scene, job, deed or outcome?

byKey.r2c1: Sentence 3 is the job Tom was given: his task, not yet an action.
byKey.r4c1: Sentence 5 is what came of his action: a result, even though it is a bad one.
byKey.r5c1: Sentence 6 is something Tom did after the loss: an action.

explain.text: Two sentences set the scene and one gives Tom his job. Three are things he did, and two say what came of them. The loss is a result too: it followed his action.

screens.prose: You used **STAR**: situation, task, action, result. Strong answers add one line of **reflection**: what you learned or would change. Tom's answer has none yet.

rows: Keep the team inside its limits
Stopped checking; then closed it, told the team, wrote a check

screens.question: Which reflection line fits Tom's story best?

options.text: "I now automate any check I would otherwise leave to memory."
"I learned that markets can be unpredictable."
options.why: You blamed the market. The loss came from a check Tom stopped doing.

options.text: "I learned that I am too much of a perfectionist."
options.why: You picked a strength in disguise. It does not match what went wrong.

options.text: "Next time I would pick teammates who watch the limits."
options.why: You moved the blame to the team. The limits were Tom's job.

hints.text: What caused the loss?
He stopped checking after day one.
The reflection names that cause and the habit that fixes it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the line that names what Tom would change.

explain.text: A reflection names the real cause and what you now do about it. Tom's cause was a check left to memory. Lines that blame luck, the team or a fake flaw sound evasive.

screens.prose: Maya answered "Tell me about a time you worked in a team." One sentence hides what she did inside what the team did.

rows: Our society ran a charity quiz for 200 people in March.
I was treasurer, so the budget was my job.
We sorted out the venue, the prizes and the tickets.
I cut the venue cost from £600 to £350 by moving to a weekday.
The quiz raised £1,900, £400 more than the year before.
I learned to book early and compare three quotes.

screens.question: Tap the sentence that hides Maya inside the team.

hints.text: Look for "we".
Sentence 3 says what the team did.
Sentence 3: who sorted the venue, the prizes or the tickets?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the sentence where you cannot tell what Maya did.

byKey.r0: That sentence sets the scene. It is not meant to hold her action.
byKey.r1: That sentence says "I was treasurer": her own role, clearly.
byKey.r3: "I cut the venue cost" is her own action, with numbers.
byKey.r4: That is the result, and it has numbers in it.
byKey.r5: That is her reflection, in the first person.

explain.text: "We sorted out the venue, the prizes and the tickets" could mean Maya did all of it or none. Say which part was yours: "I booked the venue." Interviewers hire one person, not the team.

screens.prose: Maya's result sentence is gone. Which version would an interviewer believe and remember?

rows: Our society ran a charity quiz for 200 people in March.
I was treasurer, so the budget was my job.
We sorted out the venue, the prizes and the tickets.
I cut the venue cost from £600 to £350 by moving to a weekday.
I learned to book early and compare three quotes.

screens.question: Which result sentence is strongest?

options.text: "The quiz raised £1,900, £400 more than the year before."
"The quiz went really well, and everyone enjoyed it."
options.why: You picked a feeling. Nothing in it can be counted or checked.

options.text: "People said it was the best quiz the society had run."
options.why: You picked hearsay. It is praise, not an outcome.

options.text: "It showed I am a natural leader."
options.why: You picked a claim about Maya. A result says what changed in the world.

hints.text: Which one could you check?
Look for a number and a comparison.
£1,900, and £400 more than last year.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the result an interviewer could check.

explain.text: £1,900 and £400 more can be checked and compared with last year. A feeling, a compliment or a claim about yourself gives the interviewer nothing to hold. Where no number exists, give an outcome anyone could see.

screens.prose: Nadia, an invented candidate, keeps six stories, each built for one question. Can each answer others: a mistake, leading others, persuading someone? Fill each blank with Yes or No.

rows: Momentum test; found a look-ahead bug in my own code
52% against a 70% aim; new revision plan; 71% in June
Trading game, one afternoon; chose half size with data missing
Captain; talked the team into a new plan; won 6 of 8 after
Disagreed with the manager; used sales data; waste £120 to £70
Took over accounts, never kept any, 2 weeks before a tournament

screens.question: Fill each blank: can the story answer that question?

hints.text: A story fits a question if its actions show that thing.
The look-ahead bug was in Nadia's own code.
Backtest, a mistake: Yes. Exam, leading: No. Contest, persuading: Yes. Café, persuading: Yes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read each story's few words for the thing the column asks about.

byKey.r0c1: The bug was in her own code, so the backtest is a mistake story too.
byKey.r1c2: Revising alone shows no leading of others.
byKey.r2c3: She argued the team into half size: that is persuading.
byKey.r4c3: She used sales data to change the manager's mind: that is persuading.

explain.text: Each story was built for one question but fits others. The backtest is also a mistake story, and the café dispute is also persuasion. Every column already has two or three stories.

screens.prose: Three more question types: a tight deadline, something you are proud of, learning something fast. Fill each blank with Yes or No.

rows: Momentum test; found a look-ahead bug in my own code
52% against a 70% aim; new revision plan; 71% in June
Trading game, one afternoon; chose half size with data missing
Captain; talked the team into a new plan; won 6 of 8 after
Disagreed with the manager; used sales data; waste £120 to £70
Took over accounts, never kept any, 2 weeks before a tournament

screens.question: Fill each blank: can the story answer that question?

hints.text: Look for a date or time limit, a result to be proud of, or something new learned.
The society story has "2 weeks" and "never kept any".
Backtest, deadline: No. Netball, proud of: Yes. Society: Yes and Yes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read each story's few words for the thing the column asks about.

byKey.r0c1: The backtest has no deadline in it. Another story answers that question better.
byKey.r3c2: Six wins in eight after her plan is a result to be proud of.
byKey.r5c1: Two weeks before a tournament is a deadline.
byKey.r5c3: She had never kept accounts, then kept them in two weeks: learning fast.

explain.text: All six columns now have two or more stories. So six stories, prepared well, answer most behavioural questions, which are these types in other words. Prepare the six; do not chase a list of forty questions.

screens.prose: One story can open three ways. Nadia took over the poker society's accounts two weeks before a tournament. She had never kept accounts.

rows: A time you learned something fast
A time you were trusted with money
"I hold the society's accounts for 140 members."
A time you organised an event
"I ran a tournament for 60 players, under budget."

screens.question: Which opening fits "Tell me about a time you learned something fast"?

options.text: "Two weeks before our tournament, I took over accounts I had never kept."
"I ran a tournament for 60 players, under budget."
options.why: You picked the organising opening. It skips the learning, which is what was asked.

options.text: "I hold the society's accounts for 140 members."
options.why: You picked the trust opening. The question is about how fast you learned.

options.text: "I have done lots of things in the society, like accounts and events."
options.why: You picked a list. It opens no story at all.

hints.text: Which part of the story is about learning?
She had never kept accounts, and had two weeks.
Open on the gap: two weeks, no experience.

feedback.correct: Open on the gap she had to close.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the first sentence to the question asked.

explain.text: The same events serve three questions if the first sentence points at the right part. For learning fast, open on the gap: two weeks and no experience. Then the actions show how she closed it.

screens.prose: The question is "Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone." Three candidates open differently.

rows: "In that situation, I would listen first and then explain my view."
"My weakness is that I care too much about being right."
"In March my manager wanted to cut a shift, and I thought the data said no."

screens.question: Whose opening answers the question?

options.text: Ana's: a real time, with who and when
Leo's: a calm, sensible approach
options.why: You picked the hypothetical. "I would" says what Leo might do, not what he did.

options.text: Priya's: an honest weakness
options.why: You picked a strength in disguise. It names no time and no disagreement.

options.text: None: a general approach is safer than one story
options.why: You chose the general answer. The question asks for one time.

hints.text: Which opening names a time that happened?
"I would" is about the future.
Ana's: March, her manager, a shift.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the opening that starts a real story.

byKey.leo: You picked the hypothetical answer. The question asks for a time, so "I would" tells the interviewer nothing you have done.
byKey.priya: You picked a strength dressed as a weakness. Interviewers hear it often, and it dodges the question.
byKey.none: You chose a general approach over a story. Behavioural questions are marked on what you did once.

explain.text: Behavioural questions ask about the past because past actions predict future ones. "I would" is a promise anyone can make. Start with when it happened and who was involved.

screens.prose: An edge case. Leo has no internship or society role. His strongest story is from a Saturday job in a supermarket.

rows: Stock count came out 300 items short on one aisle
I recounted shelf by shelf and found a mislabelled pallet
Fixed in 2 hours; the store kept my shelf-by-shelf method

screens.question: Is this a valid story for "Tell me about a time you solved a problem"?

options.text: Yes: the actions and the result are his
No: only study or finance stories count
options.why: You ruled out a job outside finance. Interviewers mark the actions, not the setting.

options.text: Only if he says it taught him about trading
options.why: You bolted on a trading link. A close can link to the role, but the story stands on its actions.

options.text: Yes, but he should say "we" to sound modest
options.why: You chose "we". Then the interviewer cannot tell what Leo did.

hints.text: What does STAR mark?
Look at who did the recount.
His actions, his result: valid.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the actions and the result are his.

explain.text: A shop, a sports team or caring for a relative are all valid settings. What is marked is a real problem, actions that were yours and a result. Leo's shelf-by-shelf recount is a method an interviewer can ask about.

screens.prose: Your stories share one budget. In a two-minute answer: $$\underbrace{15}_{S} + \underbrace{10}_{T} + \underbrace{60}_{A} + \underbrace{20}_{R} + \underbrace{15}_{\text{reflect}} = 120 \text{ s}$$ Half the time goes on the actions, because they are what is marked.
screens.question: At 130 words a minute, about how many words is the action part?

hints.text: What fraction of a minute is 60 s?
The action part runs from 25 s to 85 s.
One minute at 130 words a minute is 130 words.

byKey.all: That is the whole two minutes. The actions are 60 of the 120 seconds.
byKey.per-s: You used one word a second.

explain.text: $130 \times 60 / 60 = 130$ words: room for two or three specific actions. As a check, that is half the 260 words two minutes hold. Situation and task share 25 seconds, about 54 words.

screens.prose: **Follow-up.** After Tom's story the interviewer asks: "How do you know it would not happen again?" Pace: about 30 seconds, aloud.

lines: You: I then wrote a check of every position against its limit, run twice a day.
You: We finished 9th of 40 teams, and no limit was broken again.
Interviewer: How do you know it would not happen again?
params.title: End of Tom's story

screens.question: Which answer is strongest?

options.text: "The check ran 8 days with no breach, and I use it in my own backtests now."
"I am much more careful now, so it will not happen."
options.why: You gave a promise. The question asks for evidence.

options.text: "I can't know that; mistakes happen to everyone."
options.why: You dodged. Give what you can show: the check and its record.

options.text: Retell the story from the start
options.why: You retold the story. The follow-up wants one new fact.

hints.text: What could Tom point to?
Line 1: a check that runs twice a day.
Its record since, and where he still uses it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the answer that gives something checkable.

explain.text: A strong follow-up answer gives evidence: the check's record and where you still use it. "I am more careful" cannot be tested. Expect a follow-up on every story, so know one fact beyond what you said.

screens.prose: Nadia has nine experiences to choose from. A good story has actions that were hers and a result. Together her six should cover a project, a failure, a decision, a team, a disagreement and pressure.

rows: Built it alone; found a bug; net Sharpe 0.4
52% against a 70% aim; new plan; 71% in June
Chose half size with data missing; 3rd of 24
Captain; new training plan; won 6 of 8
Disagreed with the manager; waste £120 to £70
Took over the accounts 2 weeks before a tournament
Was in a group that scored 68%

screens.question: Select all that apply: which six should she turn into stories?

options.text: Momentum backtest
Probability exam
University trading game
Netball team
Café job
Poker society
Group coursework
options.why: You picked the group coursework. "Was in a group" has no action of hers in it.

options.text: A levels
options.why: You picked her grades. They are a fact for the CV, not a story with actions.

options.text: Summer reading
options.why: You picked the reading. It shows interest, but nothing happened that she had to act on.

hints.text: Which rows have an action and a result?
Rows 7 to 9 have no action of hers, or no result.
The first six: backtest, exam, trading game, netball, café, poker society.

feedback.correct: Six stories with actions and results.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the rows where she acted and something came of it.

explain.text: Each of the six has actions that were hers and a result, and together they cover the six types. Grades and reading are CV facts. You write your six in homework 3, and answer each aloud before you mark it.

ideas: A story needs a situation, a task, actions with "I", a result with a number and a reflection.
Six stories (a project, a failure, a decision, a team, a disagreement, pressure) cover most behavioural questions.
Answer with a real past event, not "I would", and say "I" for your own actions.

formula.name: Two minutes of STAR
formula.note: Half the time on actions: about 130 words.

summary.trap: Answering with "I would" instead of a real time, or a failure that is a strength in disguise.

quiz.question: Which sentence is an action, in STAR terms?

options.text: "I rewrote the cleaning script so it ran in 4 minutes."
"The project was due in two weeks."
options.why: You picked the situation. It sets the scene; no one acts in it.

options.text: "The model scored 61% accuracy."
options.why: You picked the result. It is what came of the actions.

options.text: "I was asked to clean the data."
options.why: You picked the task. It is the job, before anything was done.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the sentence where the candidate does something.

explain.text: An action is something you did, with "I" and a verb. The others set the scene, state the job or report the outcome.

quiz.question: "Tell me about a time you failed." Which failure is strongest to tell?

options.text: Missing a coursework deadline by a day through poor planning, and what you changed
"I work too hard and sometimes forget to rest"
options.why: You picked a strength in disguise. Interviewers hear it as a dodge.

options.text: A lost case competition because a teammate was late
options.why: You picked a failure that was someone else's. Yours must be yours.

options.text: "I have not really failed at anything important"
options.why: You claimed no failures. It sounds either untrue or untested.

feedback.correct: A real failure, yours, with a change.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the failure that is real and yours.

explain.text: A good failure story is real, owned and followed by a change you can show. Disguised strengths and borrowed blame are the two common dodges.

quiz.question: Select all that apply: what makes a result sentence strong?

options.text: A number
A comparison with before
An outcome anyone could see
A strong adjective such as "excellent"
options.why: You picked an adjective. It cannot be checked.

feedback.correct: A number, a comparison, an observable outcome.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep what an interviewer could check.

explain.text: A result is believed when it can be checked: a number, a before and after, or a visible outcome. Adjectives add nothing.

quiz.question: A candidate says: "We built a model that won the prize." What should they change?

options.text: Say which part was theirs: "I built the features; we won."
Nothing: "we" sounds modest
options.why: You kept "we". Modesty hides the one person being hired.

options.text: Drop the prize: it sounds boastful
options.why: You dropped the result. It is the strongest part; keep it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The interviewer needs your own actions.

explain.text: Interviewers mark what you did. Keep the team's result, but name your own part with "I".
